title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 4 (12/07/2018)
text:
TWO DECISIONS RENDERED ON 12 JULY 2018
Subject: Two identical challenge decisions were issued and concern two parallel
arbitrations. The First Respondent, appearing in both arbitrations, challenged
the Sole Arbitrator (selected by the LCIA Court) pursuant to Article 10.4 of the
LCIA Rules 1998.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of Pakistani law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to matters contained in the Sole Arbitrator’s Interim
Award in each case (which were substantially the same and in most respects
identical), and to additional remarks made by the Sole Arbitrator during the
course of the proceedings.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The seat of the arbitration was London and the challenge was determined in
accordance with English law. Although, as a matter of comity, reference may
properly be made to the laws of Pakistan (which the First Respondent argued
should apply), those laws cannot override the effect of English law which
prima facie governed the conduct of the Sole Arbitrator and the Parties seated
in London. In any event, in the LCIA Court’s view there is no material
difference, at least in relation to the issues raised by this challenge, between
the laws of England and of Pakistan.
The Sole Arbitrator’s statement that it would be “an extraordinary waste of
time and money” to revisit the issue of the seat, which had already been
determined by the LCIA Court pursuant to the LCIA Rules, even if using
unusually strong language, was accurate. The Sole Arbitrator was justified in
seeking to deter the First Respondent from further pursuing the point, which
had been decided by the LCIA Court and which was binding on the Parties and
the Sole Arbitrator.
The Sole Arbitrator’s application of English arbitral procedural law in the
Awards does not amount to an improper pre-determination of the disputed
seat issue and does not call into question the Sole Arbitrator’s impartiality in
circumstances where there can be no doubt that the proceedings were indeed
to be conducted in accordance with English arbitral procedural law.
The Sole Arbitrator’s statement that the latter “tr[ies] to make the form fit the
substance rather than the other way around” does not raise any concerns of

the application of personal knowledge or principles known only to the Sole
Arbitrator and not revealed to the Parties.
The Claimant’s adoption during the hearing of certain language used
previously by the Sole Arbitrator did not put the Sole Arbitrator in breach of
any obligation not to act as an advocate for one of the Parties.
The Sole Arbitrator’s concession of being unfamiliar with the governing law of
the contract (Pakistani law) does not evidence lack of capacity. A party relying
on any matter of foreign law, on which the Tribunal is not an expert, is entitled
to prove the law in question by appropriate evidence, but no such foreign law
principle has been identified within the Awards, and therefore the question
whether the Sole Arbitrator was familiar with the laws of Pakistan is of no
immediate relevance to the Sole Arbitrator’s role in the present arbitration.
The Sole Arbitrator’s remark that the First Respondent had not provided
evidence of attempts to settle in good faith, in the context of a hearing
scheduled to address preliminary objections and not for production of
evidence, did not effect a change of arbitral procedure and did not amount to
any “serious irregularity”.
The First Respondent’s allegations that the Sole Arbitrator had not understood
and applied the issues as revealed by the pleadings provided no support for
any finding of bias or partiality.
The First Respondent’s allegations that the Sole Arbitrator failed to address all
of the issues and failed to give sufficient reasons in the Award was not
supported by the plain reading of the Awards.
When read in context, the Sole Arbitrator’s remark that the First Respondent’s
failure to pay deposits directed by the LCIA could be relied on in the future as
evidence of the First Respondent’s general attitude towards honouring its
financial obligations, does not amount to pre-judgment of issues or lack of
impartiality or independence. While the Sole Arbitrator’s use of forceful terms
was unwise as it could give the impression of pre-judging the issue of non-
payment of the sums in the arbitration, when read in context, the comment
actually amounts to a criticism.
Decision 4 - 2

IN THE MATTER OF THE ARBITRATION ACT 1996
AND THE LCIA ARBITRATION RULES 1998
LCIA Arbitration No […]
B E T W E E N:

______________________________________
DECISION ON CHALLENGE
______________________________________
Background
1. This is the second of two substantially identical cases in which a power company as Claimant brings
claims substantially in respect of unpaid invoices against the First Respondent for power supplies
under a Power Purchase Agreement, the Second Respondent being party to an Implementation
Agreement and also Guarantor, the Respondents being common to both cases. The claims in each
case are substantial being USD 19m in the first case and USD 10.5 in the second.
2. In Arbitration [2] the Power Company is [B] who entered into a Power Purchase Agreement with the
First Respondent on 13 November 2007. In Arbitration [1] the Power Company Claimant is [A] who
entered into a Power Purchase Agreement with the First Respondent on 1 July 2008. The issues in the
two cases are substantially the same and in both cases the Request for Arbitration was registered with
the LCIA on 31 July 2017. Responses of the First Respondent in the two cases were served on 7
September 2017. Both arbitrations are governed by the 1998 LCIA Rules in accordance with the
arbitration clauses agreed by the parties.
Decision 4 - 3

3. On 19 October 2017 [Z] was appointed sole Arbitrator in both cases. No order for consolidation has
been made or requested, but the two cases have been dealt with in parallel with the parties having
the same representation and the issues presented to the Arbitrator being substantially identical. Thus
the Statements of Case were served on behalf of each Claimant on 17 December 2017; the First
Respondent raised certain objections to the institution of proceedings; on 28 December the First
Respondent served a submission against Maintainability of the Arbitration and the Second
Respondent indicated that it too would object to the Arbitrator’s jurisdiction; on 8 January 2018 a
procedural conference call took place with all parties in both cases being represented; and thereafter
both Respondents served submissions challenging the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. A hearing on
jurisdictional issues in both cases took place on 19 and 20 February 2018 and on 16 April 2018 the
Arbitrator issued his Awards in each case dismissing the challenges. Although two Awards were issued,
the arguments, the issues dealt with and the decisions were substantially the same and in most
respects identical.
4. On 10 May 2018 the First Respondent in each case filed an application under Rule 10 of the LCIA Rules
1998 (read with the laws of Pakistan) for the revocation of the Arbitrator’s appointment. The
application was accompanied by a letter of the same date addressed to the Registrar. On 12 May 2018
the Claimant, while not submitting a detailed response, disagreed with the application which was said
to be baseless. On 17 May 2018 the First Respondent responded to the Claimant’s response. On 18
May 2018 the Arbitrator responded, stating that he did not consider that he could properly withdraw
from the arbitration. On 22 May 2018 the LCIA stated that the court would be invited to decide the
challenge.
5. On 25 June 2018 the parties were notified that, pursuant to Article 10.4 of the LCIA Rules and Article
D.3(b) of the Constitution of the LCIA Court, the LCIA Court had appointed the undersigned to
determine the challenges brought by the First Respondent.
Contracts and Arbitration Clauses
6. The governing law of the Agreements is the law of Pakistan and the language of the arbitration is
English.
Decision 4 - 4

7. So far as relevant to this determination, each Power Purchase Agreement contains provision whereby
disputes may be settled by arbitration in accordance with the rules of the London Court of
International Arbitration, as in effect on the date of this Agreement by one Arbitrator appointed in
accordance with the Rules.
8. Under the LCIA Rules the Court is empowered to determine the seat of the arbitration. By email dated
19 October 2017, the LCIA informed the parties that the LCIA Court had decided, pursuant to Article
16.1 of the Rules, that the seat of the arbitration should be London.
9. Whilst both of the foregoing matters may be the subject of further challenges in a court of competent
jurisdiction, they are not matters of challenge in regard to the present application which is concerned
solely with maters arising under Article 10 of the Rules.
10. As regards the position of the Second Respondent in each case, although stated to have consented to
being joined in the arbitration, it is recorded in the Awards that it was contended that the Second
Respondent was not a party to the arbitrations and that no present liability could exist in respect of
the Second Respondent. Both contentions were dismissed with the observation that it was remarkable
that the Second Respondent would wish to be excluded from the arbitration. Again these are matters
which may be challenged in a proper court but are not relevant to the First Respondent’s application
under Article 10.
11. It is to be recorded that the Second Respondent does not in fact join or support the present application
which is opposed by the Claimant and is not accepted by the Arbitrator.
The Disputes
12. In the Requests for Arbitration, each Claimant states that the parties agreed that the Claimants would
design, engineer, construct, insure, commission, operate and maintain […] facilities for the sale and
purchase of electricity. The Claimants are obligated by the Power Purchase Agreement to supply and
sell generation capacity and electrical energy, and the First Respondent is obligated to purchase the
same, in accordance with and pursuant to the terms of the Agreements.
Decision 4 - 5

13. The First Respondent is the exclusive power purchaser and the Claimants cannot sell electrical energy
produced to any other person. The Claimants state that their income, therefore, solely depends on
the payments made by the First Respondent. The Claimants claim is for non-payment by the First
Respondent of amounts due and payable under the Agreements together with interest; and that the
Second Respondent is obligated to pay the Claimants any amount payable by the First Respondent
under the Agreements.
Grounds of Challenge
14. By its email of 10 May 2018, the First Respondent states that circumstances and reasons detailed in
the accompanying application give rise to justifiable doubts as to the impartiality and independence
of the Tribunal. The First Respondent states that it does not raise objection against the capabilities,
expertise and knowledge of the respected Arbitrator, but as set out in the application, the First
Respondent has lost confidence in the Sole Arbitrator and apprehends that he will not be able to
conduct an impartial adjudication of the dispute.
15. In the application, after reciting the “Factual Matrix”, the First Respondent sets out the “Grounds of
the Application” being in summary the following:
(a) When the First Respondent requested that the issue of the seat of the arbitration be
considered, the Arbitrator expressed surprise that the point was still being reserved
and remarked that this would be “an extraordinary waste of time and money”.
(b) The Arbitrator thereby opted to proceed with the arbitration “without affording the
parties the proper opportunity of hearing and due process” and determined the issues
in accordance with English procedural law, thus indicating pre-determination and
justifiable doubts as to the impartiality of the Tribunal.
(c) The Arbitrator is recorded as having stated that “I get hung up on principles and try to
make the form fit the substance rather than the other way around”, which indicated
that he had applied principles known only to the Arbitrator as a matter of personal
knowledge, causing substantial damage to the First Respondent and thus justifiable
doubts as to his impartiality.
Decision 4 - 6

(d) The Arbitrator in making remarks during the hearing afforded the Claimant the
opportunity of adopting what the Arbitrator had said and thus violating the rule that
an Arbitrator must not act as an advocate for any party and raising doubts as to his
independence.
(e) The Arbitrator had conceded that he was unfamiliar with the Laws of Pakistan thus
raising doubts as to his capacity.
(f) The Arbitrator remarked that the First Respondent had not provided evidence of
acting in good faith to resolve the dispute, as required by the Arbitration Agreement,
thereby changing the procedure which had been adopted, which amounted to a
serious irregularity and providing grounds for removal of the Arbitrator.
(g) The Arbitrator erroneously asserted that a matter contended for by the First
Respondent had not been pleaded indicating the Arbitrator was unaware of the
pleadings and had disregarded the procedural law of Pakistan.
(h) The Arbitrator has not addressed all the issues nor provided sufficient reasons in the
Awards.
(i) The Arbitrator in his email dated 25.04.2018 to the First Respondent stated that “I
would be surprised if this conduct is not relied on in the future as evidence of a cavalier
and irresponsible attitude generally towards honouring financial obligations which are
plain beyond dispute”. He thus became an advocate of a party, showed an incorrect
appreciation of the dispute before him, and wrongly accused the First Respondent of
a beach of its obligation, thus giving rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality.
Application of LCIA Rules
16. The applicable 1998 LCIA Rules provide as follows:
“10.2 If any Arbitrator acts in deliberate violation of the Arbitration Agreement (including these
Rules) or does not act fairly and impartially as between the parties or does not conduct or participate
Decision 4 - 7

in the arbitration proceedings with reasonable diligence, avoiding unnecessary delay or expense, that
Arbitrator may be considered unfit in the opinion of the LCIA Court.
10.3 An Arbitrator may also be challenged by any party if circumstances exist that give rise to
justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence….
10.4 A party who intends to challenge an Arbitrator shall, within fifteen days of the formation of
the Arbitral Tribunal or (if later) after becoming aware of any circumstances referred to in Article 10.1,
10.2 or 10.3, send a written statement of the reasons for its challenge to the LCIA Court, the Arbitral
Tribunal and all other parties. Unless the challenged Arbitrator withdraws or all other parties agree to
the challenge within fifteen days of receipt of the written statement, the LCIA Court shall decide on the
challenge.”
17. A challenge should thus be submitted within 15 days of becoming aware of the grounds for challenge.
The application is based substantially on the matters contained in the Interim Award dated 16 April
2018, which was notified to the parties on 25 April 2018. The challenge dated 10 May 2018 was
therefore served 15 days after delivery of the Award. In any event the Award is noted as having been
delivered at 9:03pm Lahore time, i.e. after close of business, and arguably time should run only from
the following day.
18. Some limited issues are raised which arose before the date of the Award. Those matters are arguably
out of time. Similarly matters arising from the arbitration hearing itself necessarily arose at the time
of the hearing and are arguably out of time. However for completeness all the issues are first
considered on their merits.
Consideration of grounds
19. While the grounds of challenge summarised above are those set out under the section headed
“Grounds of the Application” it is to be noted that the grounds in some cases duplicate material
contained in an earlier section headed “Factual Matrix” and are followed by submissions on the LCIA
Rules and the status in law of an Arbitrator in the particular context of the law of Pakistan. In this
regard, while English authority is also quoted it is observed that the laws of Pakistan are in many
respects similar to English law and that the laws of Pakistan provide grounds for the removal of an
Arbitrator as they were in English law before the Arbitration Act 1996. It may be noted that, apart
from certain procedural matters, the Arbitration Act 1996 has not made any material change to English
law regarding the removal of an Arbitrator. Nevertheless in the light of the stance taken by the First
Respondent it is necessary as a preliminary matter to address the question of which law is applicable
Decision 4 - 8

to the present application for revocation of the appointment of the Arbitrator under the powers
contained in Article 10 of the LCIA Rules of 1998.
20. While the First Respondent continues to object to the chosen forum of London, the decision as to
forum, as noted above, was made by the LCIA Court in accordance with the Rules and, whether or not
the First Respondent is now entitled to pursue any challenge to that decision, it is not a matter which
is open to the First Respondent under the present challenge proceedings, which are limited to claims
that there exist justifiable doubts as to the impartiality or independence of the Arbitrator.
21. Thus, for the purpose of this Decision it is to be taken that the seat of the Arbitration, as determined
by the LCIA Court, is London and it follows that any application to the LCIA Court for redress in
accordance with its rules is to be determined in accordance with the applicable procedural law,
namely English law. Whilst, as a matter of comity, reference may properly be made to the laws of
Pakistan, those laws cannot override the effect of English law which prima facie governed the conduct
of the Arbitrator and the parties seated in London. Having made this point, however, it should be
emphasised that, in my view, there is no material difference, at least in relation to the issues raised
by this challenge, between the laws of England and of Pakistan.
22. This Decision now proceeds to address the specific grounds of challenge as summarised above. The
first issue (a) arises from a remark of the Arbitrator concerning the First Respondent’s reservation of
its challenge to the seat of the Arbitration, which the Arbitrator thought to be “an extraordinary waste
of time and money”. Whilst this may be regarded as unusually strong language, it is clear from the
consideration set out above that the Arbitrator and the parties were bound by the decision of the LCIA
Court. Whatever grounds of challenge may have been open to the First Respondent, no such challenge
could be entertained by the Arbitrator and in that sense any continued objection in the course of the
arbitration was indeed a waste of time and money. The particular complaint is that the First
Respondent was not given a proper opportunity (to present its case), and thus was a breach of due
process. In my view the Arbitrator was right and was indeed justified in seeking to deter the First
Respondent from further pursuing the point.
23. The second ground of challenge (b) follows from the previous ground in that the First Respondent
complained that the Award is headed “In the matter of the Arbitration Act 1996” thus indicating a
Decision 4 - 9

predetermination of the issue of the seat and giving rise to doubts as to the impartiality of the Tribunal.
In the light of the observations above, there can be no doubt that, for the purpose of the Arbitration,
the proceedings were indeed to be conducted in accordance with the Arbitration Act 1996 and neither
this nor similar observations by the Arbitrator can be the subject of any complaint within the
arbitration nor can it found any contention as to lack of impartiality.
24. The next matter (c) concerns the observation of the Arbitrator of trying to make the “form fit the
substance”, rather than the other way round. The complaint raised is that this involves the application
of “personal knowledge or the principles known only to the Arbitrator in his personal capacity” which
is said to give rise to prejudice and justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s impartiality. However, apart
from the fact that the quotation relied on is clearly taken out of context, the First Respondent has not
drawn attention to any statement or finding contained in the Award which is said to be based on some
principle “known only to the Arbitrator in his personal capacity”. It is difficult to understand exactly
what it meant by these words but in my view there is no substance whatsoever in the contention that
the Arbitrator has adopted or made use of any principle or matter which has not been revealed to the
parties.
25. The following matter (d) concerns a statement recorded as being made by the Claimant that: “I would
go back to what you said … covering our bases and throwing the kitchen sink”. The words in question
are said to have been used by the Tribunal when the First Respondent was making its arguments which
words were subsequently adopted by the Claimant giving rise to the First Respondent’s suggestion
that the Arbitrator had thereby acted as an advocate for one of the parties (presumably the Claimant).
Such an accusation borders on the fanciful. If it is to be taken seriously it must be rejected as a wholly
unwarranted suggestion with no proper basis.
26. The next contention (e) is based on the concession by the Arbitrator of being “unfamiliar with the laws
of Pakistan” which is the governing law of the agreement. To suggest that this is evidence of lack of
capacity on the part of the Arbitrator shows a serious misunderstanding of the arbitral process. A party
relying on any matter of foreign law, that is foreign to the Tribunal, is entitled to prove the law in
question by appropriate evidence which the Arbitrator must then assess. However no such foreign
law principle has been identified within the Award itself, and therefore the question whether the
Decision 4 - 10

Arbitrator was familiar with the laws of Pakistan is of no immediate relevance to his role in the present
arbitration. This ground of challenge is to be rejected.
27. The following issue (f) concerns the approach of the Arbitrator to the issue of attempts to resolve the
dispute in good faith, which can be seen to be referred to in the Awards at paragraphs 50 and 63. The
particular complaint is that in referring to the First Respondent’s failure to produce evidence of
attempts to settle in good faith, as observed during the hearing, the Arbitrator had thereby applied a
different procedure in that the hearing had been scheduled to address preliminary objections and was
not for production or recording of evidence so that the Arbitrator’s approach amounted to a “serious
irregularity”. A perusal of the Awards reveals that the “evidence” referred to was documentary
evidence and the observation was that the First Respondent had failed to produce any such
documentary evidence. However, if it is seriously to be contended that, as a result, the procedure in
the arbitration had been changed, such a complaint should be founded on the findings within the
Awards. No complaint is advanced based on the Award and in my view there is no substance in the
suggestion that the Arbitrator had in fact changed the scheduled procedure. Indeed it is clear that the
Arbitrator’s examination of the facts was based on the documentary record as the factual matrix in
which the Contract terms were to be interpreted and applied. In my view there is no substance in this
allegation.
28. The next ground (g) concerns observations of the Arbitrator during the hearing concerning the
pleadings and the extent of the Tribunal’s understanding or appreciation of the pleaded issues. The
particular complaint of the First Respondent is first that the Tribunal was unaware of the pleadings
relating to the dispute, that the Arbitrator had not followed certain provisions of the laws of Pakistan;
that the Claimant was allowed to pursue a contention contrary to an earlier admission; and finally that
the Tribunal had failed to use reasonable dispatch in the conduct of the proceedings and the making
of the Award. These allegations are somewhat confused and confusing but the substance is that the
Arbitrator had not understood and applied the issues as revealed by the pleadings. As thus
understood, the contentions advanced give no support whatever to the allegation that the Arbitrator
thereby evinced any degree of bias or partiality. Indeed the conclusions as set out in the Award are
expressed in strong and positive terms indicating that the decision is not based on any fine or detailed
issues but that the attempts of both Respondents to challenge the jurisdiction of the Tribunal had
wholly failed.
Decision 4 - 11

29. The next (h) ground is that the Arbitrator has failed to address all of the issues and failed to give
sufficient reasons. A perusal of the Award shows that the Arbitrator has in fact set out with some care
a summary of the submissions of the First Respondent and of the issues thereby raised, followed by a
summary of the submissions and issues raised by the Second Respondent and the Claimant, all of
which are subsequently addressed in the Tribunal’s analysis of the issues. On the face of the Awards,
therefore, the issues have been fully addressed and detailed reasons presented. It is notable that the
First Respondent does not draw attention to any issue said to have been overlooked or not adequately
dealt with and in the absence of any such reference the complaint does not bear further analysis.
30. The final ground of complaint concerns an email sent by the Arbitrator on 25 April 2018 in response
to an email from the first Respondent to the LCIA Secretariat seeking further time to pay the requested
deposit of funds, in which the Arbitrator expresses himself in unusually strong language. He observes
that the parties’ behaviour “is inevitably and properly taken into account by a tribunal which is called
upon to decide whether that party is in the habit of honouring all of its obligations”. The First
Respondent complains in effect that the Arbitrator thereby demonstrates lack of impartiality as well
as an incorrect appreciation of the dispute and that the First Respondent was not in breach of any
obligation. It is notable that the amount of outstanding funding requested by the LCIA was trivial
compared to the sums alleged to be unpaid under the Power Purchase Agreement which form the
principal issues in the Arbitration, if jurisdiction is confirmed.
31. The First Respondent’s challenge, after reviewing relevant legal principles concerning bias and
impartiality in relation to all the issues raised by the application makes further reference to the
“aggressive contents and tone of the Tribunal’s email dated 25.04.2018 – suggesting that the
respected Tribunal had actually directed the attention of the Claimant as if he is an advocate in the
matter, to reasons against Respondent No. 1 and indicated that such a stance would be considered; as
well as for showing his premeditation, the Tribunal had put himself in a position that leads to a conflict
of interests and the laws. This makes the apparent bias more manifest in denial of natural justice
leading to an unenforceable award and to be rendered against the public policy of Pakistan”.
32. It may be noted that the email was written in circumstances where the Arbitrator had gone to some
lengths to deal in a timely manner with serious challenges which might bring the arbitration to a
Decision 4 - 12

premature end at the behest primarily of the First Respondent, where the parties had co-operated in
achieving an early hearing in a complex matter and where the Arbitrator had produced a detailed
award in response to many complex written and oral submissions; but the Award could not be
delivered as a result of the failure of the First Respondent to honor its financial obligation to the LCIA.
33. It is pertinent to review the full text of the email, much of which is not quoted in the application. The
email states:
“Dear [C],
Thank you for copying me in on your wholly unsatisfactory response to the LCIA.
I take the view that this latest breach of procedure and gross discourtesy to the other parties should
have been explained to everyone by one of the responsible lawyers who represents the party in breach.
The discourtesy is no fault of yours personally but in my view reflects very poorly indeed on the senior
lawyers in the team--my principal concern being that the parties, and their senior representatives show
proper respect for one another, as all did when they appeared before me.
It seems to me to be inconceivable that a Respondent of this standing is unable to comply with its
serious international financial obligations in respect of tiny sums of money be (sic) comparison with
what is at stake in this arbitration, and the present conduct must cast very serious doubt on the
question on (sic) whether that party intends to take this arbitration seriously. I would be surprised if
this conduct is not relied on in the future as evidence of a cavalier and irresponsible attitude generally
towards honoring financial obligations which are plain beyond dispute.
I expect this breach to be remedied without further delay and would remind all concerned that all a
parties’ behavior is inevitably and properly taken into account by a tribunal which is called upon to
decide whether that party is in the habit of honouring all of its obligations.”
34. The full text appears in Exhibit A-19 together with the message from [C], the manager legal of the First
Respondent, who had emailed the LCIA on 19 April in response to its request sent the previous day
for payment of the outstanding sum of £5,000 as the First Respondent’s share of the deposit in the
two arbitrations. The email of 19 April explains that the First Respondent is awaiting required
approvals for disbursement of foreign exchange and requests an extension of two weeks in order to
complete the necessary deposits. By this date the Award had already been signed by the Arbitrator
and it was clear that all parties needed to know whether the arbitration was to proceed or not. The
Arbitrator’s email thus refers to the First Respondent’s failure to pay the deposit as a breach of
procedure and a gross discourtesy “to the other parties” which should have been explained by one of
the lawyers representing the First Respondent.
Decision 4 - 13

35. The Arbitrator has chosen to use very direct language which, as contended by the First Respondent,
could be seen as giving assistance to the Claimant as well as “premeditation” (ie pre-determination)
and thus of bias and denial of natural justice. The issue for further consideration is whether the email
is indeed indicative of bias leading to justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence.
Conclusions
36. From the consideration above of the grounds of challenge it is clear that grounds (a) to (h) cannot
succeed and are to be dismissed. The final ground, however, raises a matter of greater concern in
which, on its face, the Arbitrator takes issue with the conduct of the First Respondent to the extent of
expressing the view that failing to pay the relatively trivial sums requested by the LCIA could be relied
on in the future “as evidence of a cavalier and irresponsible attitude generally towards honouring
financial obligations”, thus being directly relevant to the issues in the arbitration.
37. However, the parallel between failure to pay the LCIA deposit and the much more serious failure to
pay the huge sums allegedly due under the Power Purchase Agreement is obvious and hardly needed
to be pointed out to the parties. If raised in a subsequent hearing as the Arbitrator anticipates, such
failure may be raised as part of the behaviour of the parties which he anticipates would be “properly
taken into account by a Tribunal which is called upon to decide whether that party is in the habit of
honouring all its obligations”. Again, the parallel is obvious and, while it may be said the Arbitrator has
assisted the Claimant in making the point, drawing attention to the issue can similarly be seen as
ensuring that the First Respondent it is aware of the issue which, if the arbitration proceeds, will need
to be properly addressed and answered by the First Respondent.
38. The only issue which the Arbitrator has been concerned with up to the present point is the question
of jurisdiction and indeed whether the arbitration could proceed in London. That issue has been dealt
with fully and in a manner which, in my judgement, does not bear any serious criticism. Indeed the
Arbitrator is clearly to be commended for having dealt with complex and difficult issues in a timely
and efficient manner. The question whether the Arbitrator can now properly proceed to deal with the
principal issues in the arbitration is subject only to the effect of his email of 25.04.2018.
Decision 4 - 14

39. It may be that the Arbitrator’s decision to express himself in such forceful terms was unwise and that
it could give the impression of pre-judging the issue of non-payment of the sums which are the
principal issue in the arbitration. However, a careful reading of the email of 25.04.2018 does not, in
my view, demonstrate a pre-judgement of the issues but rather amounts to a criticism of the senior
lawyers of the First Respondent, who are charged with a failure to “show proper respect” for other
lawyers in the case who were not made aware of the First Respondent’s failure to honour its
commitments to the LCIA.
40. On balance, therefore, I do not consider that the content of the email reveal pre-judgment or other
lack of impartiality or independence but rather serious concern over the conduct of the First
Respondent and its senior lawyers. I add that this serious concern, at least in terms of the conduct of
the First Respondent, was justified. I therefore conclude that the challenge based on the Arbitrator’s
email of 25.04.2018 fails.
41. Accordingly all the challenges set forth in the application under Article 10 of the LCIA Rules dated 10
May 2018 are to be dismissed.
Decision given in London, the place of arbitration
this 12th July 2018
